entry.tamilMeaning: ஆர்வம்; அறிந்து கொள்ள அல்லது ஆராய விரும்பும் மனநிலை.
entry.englishMeaning: A strong desire to know, learn, investigate, or experience something.
entry.coreIdea: Curiosity is the mental pull toward missing knowledge or a new experience.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract noun naming the desire to discover or learn; here, that desire motivates an expedition.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive here: curiosity is presented as a reason to investigate, although curiosity can also lead to intrusive behaviour.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Adventurous and enthusiastic here: “overwhelming” and the decision to organize an expedition emphasize strong interest.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and widely usable in everyday, educational and professional English. “Nosiness” would instead criticize unwanted interest in others' affairs.

when_to_use: Describe the desire to ask questions, explore, learn, or examine something unfamiliar.
Explain a motive for research, creativity, investigation, or harmless personal interest.
when_not_to_use: Do not use curiosity to excuse invading another person's privacy.
If someone deliberately seeks private details that are none of their business, nosiness expresses criticism more directly.

advanced_nuance: Curiosity is praised in learning and science, but it can be criticized as nosiness when it crosses personal boundaries.
Curiosity can motivate a brief question or years of investigation; it does not by itself say how long the interest lasts.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Imagine a closed door with light underneath it and a strong wish to see beyond it.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Curiosity encouraged me to ask one more question and discover the real cause.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a message to a friend about a subject that arouses your curiosity. Ask one question you would like to explore; you may use a fictional interest.
memory_practice.recall_question: Which noun describes the desire to know or investigate?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which shows curiosity? A: Asking how the old clock works because you want to understand it. B: Repeating an answer without wanting to learn more. Explain your choice.

examples.context_one: Her curiosity about languages led her to study how children become bilingual.
examples.context_two: Out of curiosity, I checked how much water the garden uses each week.

natural_examples.mini_conversation: A: Why did you open the old manual? B: Pure curiosity—I wanted to see how the machine worked.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Driven by an overwhelming curiosity, she decided to organize an expedition.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: A strong desire to know, learn, investigate, or experience something.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Her strong desire to discover more motivates her to arrange an expedition. The sentence itself does not name what she wants to investigate.

mistakes_differences.correction: Correct: I have curiosity about astronomy, or I am curious about astronomy.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: I have curiosity to astronomy.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Curiosity is a desire to know; interest can also mean longer-term attention, involvement, or personal benefit.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: curiosity about + subject, or out of curiosity

records.reason: Remove extra sense and unsupported contextual detail; strengthen practice while retaining valid teaching content.

semanticReview.finding: Preserved natural examples, patterns, mistake/correction, memory cue and useful curiosity-versus-nosiness distinction. Removed unrelated object sense and unsupported diary/map details, aligned contextual meaning with unchanged header, and made practice choices concrete. Curiosity is not necessarily short-lived.

entry.englishMeaning: to examine or explore something that may be interesting or useful
entry.coreIdea: Go and see what it is like.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb meaning to visit or examine something to see what it is like; here, explore a new library.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Mildly positive here: the suggestion treats the library as potentially interesting.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Casual and inviting: “we should” proposes a shared weekend activity.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Informal and common in conversation. “Visit” is a neutral alternative for this library example.

when_to_use: Suggest exploring a new library with a friend. A model in this sense: Let us check out the free exhibition after lunch.
when_not_to_use: Check out explores something; check on verifies its state or welfare.
It is informal; examine or visit may suit a more formal recommendation.

advanced_nuance: check out: It is informal; examine or visit may suit a more formal recommendation.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Go and see what it is like.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Let us check out the free exhibition after lunch.
memory_practice.production_task: Suggest exploring a new library with a friend. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: to examine or explore something that may be interesting or useful. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which option fits the taught meaning and standard construction? A: Let us check out it. B: Let us check it out. Explain your choice, then check the correction and distinction.

examples.scenario: We should check out the new library this weekend.
examples.another_setting: Let us check out the free exhibition after lunch.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Let us check out the free exhibition after lunch.
B: Good idea; I will find its opening hours.

meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to examine or explore something that may be interesting or useful
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Go and see what it is like. Check out explores something; check on verifies its state or welfare.

mistakes_differences.important_difference: Check out explores something; check on verifies its state or welfare.

entry.englishMeaning: consistently able to be trusted or depended on
entry.coreIdea: You can count on it to work or on someone to do what they promise.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract description of dependability: the husband should consistently do what can reasonably be expected of him.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive: reliability is a valued quality; “more reliable” suggests that the present situation falls short.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Dissatisfied but focused on a desired improvement: the speaker states what they want from their husband.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and common across personal and workplace situations. Criticizing someone's reliability can still feel personal even though the word is not slang.

when_to_use: Use reliable to describe people who consistently meet reasonable expectations or keep commitments.
Use it for a service, device or source of information that you can normally depend on.
when_not_to_use: Do not use reliable merely to mean friendly: a pleasant person can still fail to keep promises.
One successful attempt does not necessarily show that something is reliable over time.

advanced_nuance: Reliable is a judgement about consistency, not perfection: even a reliable service may occasionally fail.
More reliable can express criticism indirectly, as in the source, because it suggests that current performance is not dependable enough.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a promised task completed on time, again and again.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Our reliable neighbour waters the plants whenever we are away.
memory_practice.recall_question: What does calling someone reliable tell you about their commitments?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Who is more reliable? A: A friendly driver who often fails to arrive. B: A quiet driver who arrives at the agreed time every day. Explain which evidence matters.
memory_practice.production_task: Recommend a fictional colleague for a time-sensitive task. Use reliable and give one concrete reason.

examples.example_1: Mina is reliable: she always sends the figures by the agreed time.
examples.example_2: We need a reliable bus service so that staff can arrive before the shop opens.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Who can collect the keys on Friday?
B: Ask Arun. He's reliable and has never missed a pickup.
A: I'll check whether he's free.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: "What  I  want  is  for  my  husband  to  be  more  reliable.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: consistently able to be trusted or depended on
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker wants her husband to be someone she can depend on more consistently. The excerpt does not identify a particular broken promise.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “She is a reliably colleague.” An adjective, not an adverb, describes the noun colleague.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “She is a reliable colleague.” Use reliably with a verb: “She reliably meets deadlines.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Reliable means dependable. Trustworthy often emphasizes honesty; a person may be honest but poorly organized and unreliable about time.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: a reliable + person/service/source; subject + be/become + reliable

records.reason: Replace generic teaching prose with specific same-sense material.

semanticReview.finding: Dependability examples vary between person and service without adding a new sense. Trustworthiness distinguished from reliability, and no absent event is invented for the source.

entry.tamilMeaning: ஒன்றின் மீது ஒருவருக்கோ ஒரு அமைப்பிற்கோ மட்டுமே இருக்கும் தனியுரிமை அல்லது கட்டுப்பாடு
entry.englishMeaning: exclusive control over a service, activity, or resource
entry.coreIdea: One person or group has something exclusively.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract idea of exclusive possession or control, extended here to fear: hospitals are not the only places where people are afraid.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral as a concept of exclusivity; the negative subject here is fear.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Emphatic and explanatory: “of course” presents the point as obvious and broadens the discussion beyond hospitals.
meaning_usage_profile.register: “Have a monopoly on” is natural in general commentary as well as business writing; this example is not an economic market definition.

when_to_use: Use have a monopoly on to say that a person or group has exclusive control of something.
Use no monopoly on or not have a monopoly on to reject a claim that a quality or experience belongs only to one group.
when_not_to_use: Do not use monopoly merely to mean being good at something; it adds the idea of exclusivity.
When speaking about experiences such as fear, make clear that the expression is figurative rather than a claim of legal ownership.

advanced_nuance: In the source, monopoly extends the idea of exclusive control to an emotion. It does not claim that fear is bought or sold.
No monopoly on often challenges an exclusive claim without denying that the named group possesses the quality at all.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a sign saying 'Only us', then remove it when others share the quality.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Our team has no monopoly on useful ideas.
memory_practice.recall_question: If hospitals have no monopoly on fear, can people feel afraid elsewhere?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which matches 'no monopoly on wisdom'? A: Only this group can be wise. B: Other groups can be wise too. Explain what no changes.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a respectful reply to a fictional manager who thinks only senior staff can solve problems. Use no monopoly on to invite wider participation.

examples.example_1: Senior managers do not have a monopoly on good ideas; junior staff can offer solutions too.
examples.example_2: No generation has a monopoly on courage.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Only our design team can suggest changes to the product.
B: We don't have a monopoly on good ideas. Let's ask the support team too.
A: Fair point. I'll invite them.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Of  course,  hospitals  don't  have  a  monopoly  on  fear.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: exclusive control over a service, activity, or resource
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer says fear is not limited to hospitals. Other places and situations can also make people afraid; hospitals do not have exclusive possession of fear.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Saying “She has a monopoly on good ideas” simply because she has many ideas suggests that nobody else has them.
mistakes_differences.correction: Use monopoly for exclusivity: “She has excellent ideas, but she has no monopoly on them.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Having an advantage means being in a better position. Having a monopoly on something suggests exclusive possession or control, a stronger claim.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: have a monopoly on + noun; have no monopoly on + noun
